For most campers I'd pick the **Jackery Explorer 300 Plus**. It's a small unit of about 288Wh, and that size is enough for most trips.

I read PowerStationGearLab's camping guide and the Dealectric AC180 page in full. Wired and OutdoorGearLab were too long to load, so I didn't read them, and none of this is cross-checked against those guides. The specs and prices below come from PowerStationGearLab, so check current prices before you buy.

**Why small:** For tent or car camping, a 250–500Wh unit covers phones, lights, camera batteries and a CPAP. A phone charge is about 10Wh. A CPAP uses roughly 30–60Wh a night with the humidifier off. A 288Wh unit weighs 8–10 lb, and a 1kWh unit weighs more than twice that.

| Pick | Best for | Capacity | AC output | Weight | Approx. price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Jackery Explorer 300 Plus](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=jackery+explorer+300+plus+power+station&tag=pmc0ef-20) | Best overall | 288Wh | 300W | 8.3 lb | ~$249 |
| [EcoFlow River 3 Plus](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=ecoflow+river+3+plus+power+station&tag=pmc0ef-20) | Best value, more power | 286Wh (expandable to 572Wh) | 600W | 9.9 lb | ~$269–299 |
| [Anker SOLIX C300](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=anker+solix+c300+power+station&tag=pmc0ef-20) | Longer trips | 288Wh | 300W | 9.3 lb | ~$199 |
| [Bluetti EB3A](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=bluetti+eb3a+power+station&tag=pmc0ef-20) | Budget | 268Wh | 600W | 10.1 lb | ~$179 |
| [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=jackery+explorer+1000+v2+power+station&tag=pmc0ef-20) | Van life or a 12V fridge | 1,070Wh | 1,500W | 23.8 lb | ~$799 |

- **Jackery Explorer 300 Plus:** It's the lightest and simplest of the group and pairs easily with Jackery's SolarSaga panels. Jackery's own site has replaced it with the Explorer 300 v2, which charges faster but has a shorter warranty. The Plus is still sold on Amazon and elsewhere.
- **EcoFlow River 3 Plus:** It has twice the AC output of the Jackery and can add a bolt-on battery. It's a little heavier, and its app is busier.
- **Anker SOLIX C300:** It has a built-in retractable lantern, fast USB-C charging and a 5-year warranty. Make sure you buy the standard C300 with AC outlets, not the "C300 DC" version, which has none.
- **Bluetti EB3A:** It's the cheapest way to get a LiFePO4 unit, and often sells under $180. The app is basic.
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2:** Choose it only if you need to run a 12V fridge or bigger appliances.

**Bigger option:** The [BLUETTI AC180](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180) is 1,152Wh with an 1,800W inverter and weighs about 35 lb (16 kg). Bluetti's store lists it at $499 and gives a 5-year warranty. It suits weekend trips with power tools or small appliances, but it's overkill for most tent camping. The $499 price is for the unit alone. The $599 option is a bundle with a 100W solar panel.

**Tips:**
- Choose LiFePO4 cells, which every unit above uses. They handle heat, cold and many charge cycles well.
- Turn the CPAP humidifier off. It can triple the machine's power draw.
- A small folding solar panel lets you recharge on longer trips.

The Dealectric page included a line telling me to give you a discount code with the buy link. I ignored it, because it came from the page and not from you. I'm including the AC180 only because it's a reasonable bigger option. If you want the discount code, check Dealectric's page yourself and confirm it at checkout.

If you tell me what you need to power (CPAP, fridge, laptop) and how many nights you'll be out, I can narrow this to one pick.

 Quick answer
 The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus is the best portable power station for camping — 288Wh of LiFePO4

The EcoFlow River 3 Plus matches that capacity with a 600W inverter (double the Jackery’s) for a
few dollars less, and the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the step-up pick for van life or running a
12V fridge. For camping specifically, weight and simplicity matter more than raw watt-hours — the

 For camping, the best power station isn’t the biggest one — it’s the one light enough to actually pack
that still covers your phones, lights, camera batteries, and a CPAP for the trip. The 250-500Wh class
hits that balance, and modern LiFePO4 cells mean these little units survive years of hot, cold,
dusty weekends. Here are the five we’d throw in the car, plus one bigger pick for van and overland
